http://www.jamaicantimes.com/news/279225.text: Devesh Uttam appointed as next Ambassador to Ethiopia ANI 06 Aug 2026, 20:59 GMT+10 New Delhi [India], August 6 (ANI): Devesh Uttam has been appointed as the next Ambassador of India to Ethiopia, the Ministry of External Affairs said on Thursday. Uttam, who joined the Indian Foreign Service in 2003, is presently Ambassador of India to Lithuania, and has been appointed as the next Ambassador of India to Ethiopia. He is expected to take up the assignment shortly. As per the website of the Indian Embassy in Vilnius, Ambassador Uttam was Head of the Consular, Passport & Visa (CPV) Division in the Ministry of External Affairs, New Delhi. He was also in charge of the Office of the Central Authority for Extradition Matters. His diplomatic assignments abroad included Deputy Chief of Mission at the Embassy of India, Tehran; and Counsellor at the Permanent Mission of India to the United Nations in New York. While in New York, he was also elected to serve as a Member of the United Nations Advisory Committee on Administrative and Budgetary Questions (ACABQ) from 2013 to 2016. He also served as India's representative on the Advisory Board of the UN Democracy Fund during his tenure in New York. Besides, he has also served in Indian Missions in Libya and Syria. He headed the Political and Commercial wings at the Embassy of India, Tripoli and the Culture and Information wing at the Embassy of India, Damascus At the Ministry of External Affairs, besides Joint Secretary, CPV Division, he has served in different Capacities including Director (Administration) and Under Secretary / Deputy Secretary (Gulf). Before joining the Indian Foreign Service, he served as Assistant Director General of Foreign Trade in the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, Government of India. He holds Master's and M.Phil. degrees from Jawaharlal Nehru University, New Delhi. His area of research in M.Phil. was the 'Eastern Enlargement of the European Union'. The focus of the study was the cost-benefit analysis for new Member States joining the EU. He has also studied International Business at the Indian Institute of Foreign Trade (IIFT), New Delhi. He speaks Hindi, English and Arabic. He has also studied French and Sanskrit. Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Two faculty members in Tennessee Tech University’s School of Music recently represented the university on the international stage with a performance at the 58th International Horn Symposium in Kraków, Poland. Gözde Çakır Ramsey, assistant professor of flute at Tech and principal flutist of the Tech-affiliated Bryan Symphony Orchestra, and Justin Stanley, assistant professor of horn and principal horn of the BSO, performed as the Center Hill Duo at the symposium. The International Horn Symposium, held in July at the Krzysztof Penderecki Academy of Music, brought together horn performers, teachers, students, composers and scholars from around the world. This year marked the first time the symposium was held in Central Europe. For Çakır Ramsey and Stanley, the performance marked their second consecutive appearance at the International Horn Symposium. The duo previously performed at the 57th International Horn Symposium in 2025 at James Madison University in Virginia. “We were honored to represent Tennessee Tech at such a prestigious international gathering of musicians and educators,” Çakır Ramsey said. “Performing alongside artists and scholars from around the world provided an incredible opportunity to share our music, learn from our colleagues and build meaningful connections through music.” As the Center Hill Duo, Çakır Ramsey and Stanley presented works by composers Katherine Hoover, Eric Ewazen and Georges Barboteu. The program highlighted the distinctive combination of flute and horn, an uncommon pairing in chamber music. The contrasting timbres, projection and volume of the flute and horn present unique challenges for performers, requiring careful attention to balance and blend. The duo uses those differences to explore a broad range of sounds in its performances. While in Kraków, the Center Hill Duo also collaborated with Olga Tsymbaluk, piano professor at the Krzysztof Penderecki Academy of Music. Tsymbaluk joined the duo for a performance, adding piano to the ensemble. Despite having only 45 minutes to rehearse together, the musicians were able to prepare the full program and perform successfully, thanks in part to Tsymbaluk’s musicianship and collaborative approach. The Kraków performance is only the latest artistic engagement for faculty in Tech’s School of Music, which presents more than 200 concerts and recitals each year and saw a nearly 72% enrollment increase between 2021 and 2025. Audiences can next see Çakır Ramsey and Stanley perform at the Bryan Symphony Orchestra’s free outdoor community concert Sunday, Sept. 6, in Cookeville’s Dogwood Park. Family activities and vendor stations open at 5:30 p.m., and the concert performance begins at 7 p.m. Learn more about the Tennessee Tech School of Music at www.tntech.edu/music . http://www.bignewsnetwork.com/news/27928.text: Big News Network.com Estonian defense minister quits after wasting 70 million on faulty shells for Ukraine Tallinn made multiple advance payments to a company with no artillery ammo-making experience, receiving "useless" product after repeated delays Estonian Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur has announced his resignation after it emerged that Tallinn had paid some 70 million ($81 million) in advance for artillery shells for Ukraine to a company with no track record of producing such ammunition. The scandal erupted on Wednesday after the Eesti Ekspress newspaper reported on the botched procurement and the ensuing legal dispute. In August 2024, Tallinn signed a contract with Italian-registered Datasel, owned by Indian company Neco Defence Munitions, to supply artillery ammunition for Ukraine. The government paid 15 million upfront despite neither company having any previous record of manufacturing artillery shells. A second deal followed in October, with Estonia paying another 10 million in advance. The first batch was due to reach Ukraine in November, but Datasel reported problems and repeatedly delayed delivery. Despite the setbacks, Estonia signed two more contracts with the company, eventually bringing total advance payments to around 70 million. The money came from the EU's European Peace Facility, which has been extensively used to fund weapons and other military assistance for Kiev. Tallinn is now disputing the contracts in a case before the European Court of Arbitration in Strasbourg in a bid to get money back. The government acknowledged the blunder, with Pevkur proclaiming the readiness to take the "political responsibility" and announcing his resignation. The outgoing minister, who will stay in the role until a replacement is picked, however, appeared to shift the blame for the affair on the country's procurement authority, the Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK). "The defense minister does not conduct contract negotiations. The defense minister does not count socks and ammunition. The defense minister makes the fundamental decision to support Ukraine," Pevkur explained. The RKIK boss, Elmar Vaher, acknowledged that his agency was to blame for the scandal, yet shifted responsibility to his predecessor, Magnus-Valdemar Saar. "I have been familiar with the matter since January. I cannot see inside people's heads to know how they were thinking and what the main arguments behind their decisions were," Vaher told the ERR broadcaster. "The decision was made by RKIK's former director general." It remained unclear to what extent the contracts remained unfulfilled, since Estonian officials provided conflicting accounts on the matter. Pevkur said that "tens of millions of euros' worth of the ammunition" were delivered and are currently sitting "in a warehouse in a European country." The shells, however, were "not of sufficient quality" to send them into Ukraine, according to the outgoing minister. The defense ministry's secretary general, Kaimo Kuusk, described the consignment as "wholly incomplete," while the Eesti Ekspress report called the munitions "useless" and faulty. https://www.dw.com/en/avalanche-in-nepal.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NMbF The Himalayas in Nepal are home to many peaks popular with tourist climbers from around the globe [FILE: April 17, 2026] Image: Elisa Schu/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement Two people have died when an avalanche struck the base camp of a mountain in Nepal with at least 14 others still missing. The avalanche hit the 7,126-meter (23,380-foot) Himlung Himal after several days of heavy rain and snowfall across the region. The dead and missing are all mountain guides and staff of Nepalese expedition companies who had been preparing the base camp for paying customers to climb the mountain. "There were a total of 14 kitchen staff members and two climbing guides from different companies who were missing," the Nepal National Mountain Guide Association said. "The two climbing guides have been found, but sadly, both were found deceased." Unclear how many are missing There was conflicting information as to how many people were in the affected area near the border with Tibet at the time of disaster. Local police said there were at least 22 people at the base camp when the avalanche struck on Sunday morning. Bibhuti Chand Thakur, head of trekking company Himalayan Holidays Nepal, told news agency DPA that search and rescue operations were under way. "The chance of survival remains high because of fresh snow," he said, adding that he did not yet have a definitive number of missing or survivors, as the area is remote and cut off from communication. While Mount Everest (pictured) is Nepal's most famous peak, peaks like Himlung Himal are also popular with climbers [FILE: May 21, 2024] Image: Narendra Shahi Thakuri/dpa/picture alliance Authorities had warned of severe weather across Nepal over the weekend. Rain has affected much of the country since Thursday, with snowfall reported in the higher northern regions. The conditions have disrupted roads and trekking routes and led authorities to suspend climbing and trekking activities on several mountains. The Himalayan nation is home to eight of the world's 14 mountains higher than 8,000 meters, and trekking and mountaineering tourism is vital to the country's economy. The latest avalanche comes as Nepal continues to recover from devastating floods in August that killed more than 1,400 people and left thousands missing.
